sources.title: N. R. Narayana Murthy (Q1398708) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-24): English label 'N. R. Narayana Murthy', description 'Indian businessman', Korean label '나라야나 무르티', born 20 August 1946, no death date, citizenship India. Orientation only; not used as support for any row. (The search for 'Narayana Murthy' alone also returns an unrelated film actor; this item is the Infosys co-founder, confirmed by its date of birth and occupation claims.)

Chris Trimble, 'Infosys: Maintaining an Edge', Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth case no. 2-0026 (2008, read in full as PDF): the 1981 founding with 10,000 rupees pooled from family and six co-founders, the first computer waiting a full year for government permission, over 200 trips to Delhi government offices in the 1980s against one in the 1990s, early attempts at the global delivery model with code sent by courier and fax, the first direct data link to the United States in 1989, deregulation and falling telecom costs in the 1990s, Murthy's description of the model as splitting work between on-site and remote activities, revenue growth of over 80 percent a year from 1998 to 2001, and the 1999 NASDAQ listing. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Academic teaching case by an outside professor; it quotes Murthy's own statements for values and the model, which are treated as self-account, while the historical sequence is the author's.

'Infosys Technologies Ltd. History', International Directory of Company Histories vol. 38 (St. James Press, 2001), reproduced by FundingUniverse (read in full): 1981 founding, 1987 first US office, 1992-1993 Indian public offerings, SEI capability-maturity certifications, the offshore and Global Delivery Model, repeat-business share, the 11 March 1999 NASDAQ listing as the first India-registered company on a US exchange, the employee stock option plan using ADRs, and fiscal 1998-2000 revenue figures. Reference-work company history compiled from trade-press reports; independent of the company's own narration but second-hand.

Asia Society, 'Mr. Narayana Murthy and Infosys: A Case Study of Indian Values' (read in full): Infosys's founding in 1981, the March 1999 NASDAQ listing, Murthy's own interview answers about a 1990 meeting at which colleagues considered a buy-out offer, introducing higher salaries and a stock option plan to keep staff, and his statements on transparency to investors. Mostly the subject's own interview answers presented by a think-tank; counted as self-account and used only with other sources.

Bloomberg (via Gulf News), 'Investors lose $3.5b as Infosys ex-CEO spars with founder', 2017 (read in full): Vishal Sikka's resignation after a year of acrimony between the board and founders led by Murthy; the founders' questions on Sikka's pay, executive severance and the Panaya acquisition; the Infosys statement blaming Murthy's 'continuous assault' and calling his letter factually inaccurate; Murthy's reply that his concern was the deteriorating standard of corporate governance; Murthy as CEO for two decades to 2002 and his return in 2013. Wire report carrying both sides, including the board's counter-voice.

Outlook India (PTI), 'My Main Concern Was Board's Poor Governance, Not Personal Gain, Says Narayana Murthy', 30 August 2017 (read in full): Murthy's investor-call account of his objections to the severance paid to a former chief financial officer and to the handling of the Panaya investigation, the board's earlier statement calling his campaign 'misguided', the board resignations and Nandan Nilekani's return as chairman, and the founders' 12.75 percent stake. News agency report of the subject's own statements alongside the board's accusation; his motives are as he states them.

YourStory, 'The year that was at Infosys: Tussle took spotlight as Founder took on CEO', 30 December 2017 (read in full): the 2014 handover to Sikka, differences in style between Murthy and Sikka over strategy, the Panaya and Skava acquisitions and the CFO severance, the board calling his letter factually inaccurate, over 70 former employees petitioning against the board's treatment of him, and the writer's judgment that Murthy was right to ask questions but that the dispute damaged the company. Startup-press retrospective; mixed supportive and critical commentary.

Wikimedia Commons file page '31. ISC-Symposium-N.R. Narayana Murthy-HSGN 028-01586.jpg' (live check 2026-10-24) -- checked for the portrait: photograph from the University of St. Gallen archive, 2001, CC BY-SA 4.0.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_nrn_tuck, src_nrn_funduni | 1981-1999 | academic case + reference company history] The Tuck case says Murthy saw in 1981 an opening to serve developed-world clients at low cost with Indian engineers and that, once deregulation and cheaper telecom links arrived in the early 1990s, the delivery model became a competitive advantage; the company history records the 1999 NASDAQ listing, used to introduce a stock option plan. The sequence is documented by outsiders, but the account of what he saw in 1981 rests on the company's own telling, so a moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 70 / 0.62 lowered to 66 / 0.55 because the 1981 motive reaches the case from the company's own narration.

persistence.rationale: [src_nrn_tuck, src_nrn_asiasoc | 1981-1990 | academic case + think-tank interview] The Tuck case records a year's wait for government permission to buy the first computer and over 200 visits to Delhi government offices in the 1980s; Murthy's interview adds that in 1990 colleagues considered a buy-out offer and he argued to continue. The licensing waits are independently documented while the 1990 episode is his own account, so a moderate-low confidence.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_nrn_bloomberg, src_nrn_tuck, src_nrn_funduni | 1981-2014 | wire report + academic case + reference history] Bloomberg describes his two decades as chief executive to 2002 and a return in 2013; the Tuck case and company history describe the growth from a start-up to a NASDAQ-listed company with revenue growing over 80 percent a year in 1998-2001, with Murthy as chairman at the 2006 anniversary. Sustained executive leadership is documented, but the sources credit a team of founders and do not describe how he led people, hence a moderate-low confidence.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_nrn_bloomberg, src_nrn_outlook, src_nrn_yourstory | 2016-2017 | wire report + news-agency report + startup press] In 2017 Murthy pressed the board publicly over executive pay, a former CFO's severance and the Panaya acquisition; the board called his campaign misguided and blamed him for the chief executive's resignation, while over 70 former employees petitioned in his support and the board later changed. Persistence in an open dispute with his own former company is documented from both sides; whether the cause was sound is contested in the sources and his motives are as he states them, so the impact is dual-edged with moderate confidence.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_nrn_tuck | 1981-1989 | academic case] The case says the company started with 10,000 rupees, could not afford a mainframe and ran mainframe simulators on personal computers, and worked around limited communications with code sent by courier and fax before the first direct data link in 1989. It describes the company's workarounds rather than Murthy's own acts and rests on one source, so a modest score at low confidence.

portrait.source: Wikimedia Commons, '31. ISC-Symposium-N.R. Narayana Murthy-HSGN 028-01586.jpg' -- portrait photograph of N. R. Narayana Murthy at the 31st St. Gallen Symposium, 2001, from the University of St. Gallen archive (Universitätsarchiv St.Gallen, reference HSGN 028/01586). The Commons page states that media uploaded by the archive are released under CC BY-SA 4.0 and records a volunteer-reviewed permission ticket from the copyright holder (live check 2026-10-24). Original 1400 x 2100 pixels (1.74 MB; stored with an orientation flag, rotated upright on processing); stored file downscaled once to 800 x 1200, no crop, never upscaled. Caveats: the licence rests on the archive's statement on Commons and the permission ticket, which could not be inspected here. Alternatives not used: the 2014 'Narayana Murthy CIF' file (own-work upload, camera date wrong, only 529 x 771 in the cropped version) and Indian government photographs (open licence but taken at political meetings).

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-24) for Q1398708 returned en label 'N. R. Narayana Murthy', description 'Indian businessman', ko label '나라야나 무르티', born 1946-08-20, no death date, citizenship India (the film actor Q7273881 is a different person). SLUG/QID CHECK: no data-pipeline candidate or src file for slug n-r-narayana-murthy or QID Q1398708. REGION: south_asia. VOCABULARY: occupations entrepreneur, executive; fields business, technology; tags founder, leader; archetypes entrepreneurial_builder, organizational_leader are existing labelled ids. ZERO POLITICS: government roles, committee chairmanships, political meetings and policy advocacy are not scored; Delhi permit visits appear only as a business-licensing obstacle. LIVING SUBJECT: public documented business conduct only. Excluded: family and marriage (including the source of the start-up capital), wealth and philanthropy, health, his later remarks on working hours, and any inferred motive for the 2017 dispute beyond his own stated position. PORTRAIT PREFLIGHT: St. Gallen archive file with CC BY-SA 4.0 and a permission ticket; found. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Chris Trimble, 'Infosys: Maintaining an Edge', Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth case (read in full). READ (7 cited non-Wikidata sources): Tuck case, FundingUniverse company history, Asia Society interview piece, Bloomberg report, Outlook/PTI report, YourStory retrospective, plus the Commons page for the portrait. Not opened or blocked: ICMR case studies (paywalled, only the free index page returned nothing usable), Harvard/INSEAD cases, Management Today (page returned almost no text), Infosys SEC filings, Britannica, books by others. PERSPECTIVES: academic case study (Tuck), reference company history (St. James Press), wire and national press carrying both Murthy's and the board's positions (Bloomberg, PTI, YourStory), and Murthy's own interview (Asia Society, self-account). Independent behavioural support: Tuck case, company history and Bloomberg. COUNTER-VOICES: the Infosys board's statements that his campaign was misguided and factually inaccurate (Bloomberg, PTI, YourStory), and the YourStory writer's view that the dispute tarnished the company. SELF-CALIBRATION: reviewed opportunity_sensing (lowered, see row), persistence (kept at 62 / 0.5: the independent licensing evidence stands, the 1990 episode is only a minor part) and conflict_tolerance (kept: both sides documented, confidence already moderate-low and impact dual-edged). No row on persuasiveness, decisiveness or collaboration because the support is his own statements. PORTRAIT: see portrait.source.
